subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Maillard Reaction
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Maillard Reaction.

hook.text: The Maillard reaction is why bread browns, steak sears, and coffee develops its rich, complex flavors.

buildup.text: When amino acids and sugars are heated together above 140°C, they form hundreds of new flavor molecules.

discovery.text: In coffee, the Maillard reaction creates melanoidins—brown polymers responsible for body, color, and that roasty aroma.

twist.text: The reaction is non-enzymatic—it happens purely from heat. No living process is required, just temperature and time.

climax.text: Over 1,000 volatile compounds are created during coffee roasting. Most come from the Maillard reaction alone.

punchline.text: Sugars plus amino acids plus heat. One reaction creates a thousand flavors.

quiz.question: What does the Maillard reaction create in coffee?
options: Melanoidins—brown polymers for body, color, and roasty aroma

details.summary: The Maillard reaction occurs when amino acids and reducing sugars interact under heat, creating hundreds of new flavor compounds. In coffee roasting this reaction produces the brown color, nutty aromas, and complex sweetness that define a well-roasted bean.
details.whyItMatters: The Maillard reaction is responsible for much of what we love about coffee aroma and flavor. Controlling it is the key to unlocking sweetness without bitterness.
takeaways: Amino acids and sugars react to form brown flavor compounds
It produces caramel, nutty, and chocolate-like notes in coffee
Temperature control during this phase shapes the cup profile

faq.question: Is the Maillard reaction the same as caramelization in coffee?
faq.answer: No. The Maillard reaction requires amino acids and sugars, while caramelization involves only sugars heated past their melting point. Both contribute to browning, but they produce different sets of flavor compounds.

faq.question: At what temperature does the Maillard reaction begin in coffee?
faq.answer: The Maillard reaction in coffee generally starts around 150 degrees Celsius (300 degrees Fahrenheit) and accelerates as bean temperature rises. It overlaps with caramelization, which begins slightly later.
